function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m happy to walk you through what you’d need to do, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone a repository, run `git` commands, or push to GitHub from here. What I can do is:

1. **Explain the steps you’d run locally**  
2. **Show you the exact files you’d create/modify** (Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, GitHub‑Actions workflow)  
3. **Give you the shell commands you’d use to stage, commit, and push**  

Below is a complete “recipe” you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or adapt to your own workflow).

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# SSH key must be set up on your machine and added to GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you prefer HTTPS, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` and make sure you’re authenticated.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create/update files

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Run a quick check to see what’s inside:

```bash
tree -L 2
```

Typical output for a minimal Node.js project might look like:

```
├── package.json
├── src
│   └── index.js
└── README.md
```

If the repo already contains a `Dockerfile`, `k8s/` folder, or `.github/workflows/` folder, you’ll want to update those; otherwise you’ll create them.

---

### 2.2 Create / Update the Dockerfile

Below is a **minimal, production‑ready Dockerfile** for a Node.js app that listens on port `3000`.  
Feel free to adjust the base image or ports if your app differs.

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Build step (if you have a build script)
# RUN npm run build

# Runtime image
FROM node:18-alpine

WORKDIR /app

# Copy only the built artifacts + node_modules
COPY --from=builder /app .

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses a multi‑stage build to keep the final image small.  
> * Installs only production dependencies (`npm ci --only=production`).  
> * Exposes port `3000` – change if your app uses a different port.  
> * Starts the app with `node src/index.js` – adjust if your entry point differs.

If you already have a Dockerfile, replace its contents with the snippet above (or merge as needed).

---

### 2.3 Create Kubernetes YAML files

Create a directory for Kubernetes manifests:

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
```

#### Deployment (`k8s/deployment.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change to your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
```

#### Service (`k8s/service.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What to change?**  
> * `image:` – point to the image you’ll publish (e.g., GitHub Container Registry).  
> * `replicas:` – scale as needed.  
> * `targetPort:` – matches the port exposed by the Dockerfile.

---

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory and file:

```bash
mkdir -p .github/workflows
cat > .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml <<'EOF'
name: Build and Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Cache node modules
      uses: actions/cache@v4
      with:
        path: ~/.npm
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-node-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
EOF
```

> **Why this workflow?**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds the Docker image using Buildx.  
> * Pushes to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`).  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication (no extra secrets required).  
> * Caches `node_modules` to speed up subsequent builds.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new/updated files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/*.yml
```

If you modified an existing file, just `git add` that file instead of creating a new one.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit and push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **Note:**  
> * If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.  
> * Make sure you have write access to the repository.

---

## 🎉 Done!

Once the push completes, GitHub Actions will automatically pick up the new workflow, build the Docker image, and push it to the registry. Your Kubernetes manifests are ready to be applied with `kubectl apply -f k8s/`.

---

### Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Dockerfile present in repo root |
| ✅ | `k8s/deployment.yaml` & `k8s/service.yaml` exist |
| ✅ | `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml` exists |
| ✅ | Files staged (`git status`) |
| ✅ | Commit made (`git log -1`) |
| ✅ | Push successful (`git push`) |

---

Let me know if you hit any snags or need help tweaking the Dockerfile/K8s configs for your specific app!
